HAIL: Companies building smarter ways to move: electric vehicles, self-driving sensors, chips for cars, batteries and transport software. Technology and consumer vehicle makers split most of the fund, making it a growth bet on the future of transportation rather than on today's car industry.
MOTG: Companies around the world with wide moats, durable advantages like brands, patents and networks that keep competitors at bay, selected by Morningstar's analysts. It blends growth and value across industries, looking for strong businesses at sensible prices.
RULE: A flexible portfolio that currently leans hard into chip and technology stocks, with room to hold bonds, cash and other funds as conditions change. Few rules bind the managers, so it can adapt quickly, for better or worse, when markets shift.
BUYO: Small and mid-sized stocks chosen to resemble the companies private equity firms buy, with similar size, cash flow and industry traits. It offers a stock-market stand-in for buyout investing, without the lockups, but also without private equity's control over its companies.
VRAI: Income from real assets: oil and gas producers, property trusts, utilities and pipelines, mostly US-listed. It aims for dividends and inflation resilience from hard-asset businesses, and energy prices drive much of its movement.
BTCC: Options on a bitcoin fund, sold to generate income while the cash sits in Treasury bills. It turns bitcoin's volatility into regular payouts, with gains limited by the options and losses cushioned only by the income collected.
TSEP: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each September. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
SOEZ: Direct exposure to Solana, the cryptocurrency of a fast blockchain network, held as the fund's sole asset. It lets investors follow Solana's price through a brokerage account, and that price is extremely volatile, driven by crypto sentiment and network adoption.
INDE: Actively managed Indian companies, led by banks and financial firms, with consumer, industry and health care names behind. It is a single-country growth bet on India's expanding economy, with the currency and political risks that come with it.
SMHC: Twenty-five of the largest, most traded Chinese semiconductor companies, from chip designers to equipment makers, bought mainly through mainland A-shares. It is a direct bet on China's push for chip independence, and tensions with the US can move it sharply.
RDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the Russell 2000 small-cap index using options that expire the same day they are sold. It targets weekly income from small-cap volatility, with gains capped and losses close to the index's own when small stocks fall.
VBCG: Corporate bonds from banks, drugmakers, technology firms and other big issuers that mature around 2033, when the fund itself is set to end. It works much like a single bond with a target end date: collect interest, then principal comes back as bonds mature.
AMZP: An options income strategy on a single stock, Amazon, using contracts tied to its shares while most assets sit in Treasury bills. It pays regular distributions from selling options, but gains are capped and it rides entirely on Amazon's stock.
COYY: Options tied to Coinbase, the big US crypto exchange, used through a related fund structure to produce boosted income payouts. It cashes in on the wild swings in crypto-linked shares, with gains capped and deep drops only partly softened by income.
VUS: US companies that pay dividends, led by technology at about two fifths, with finance, health care and property firms behind. It aims for income plus growth from established payers, and its big tech weight makes it livelier than old-style dividend funds.
NBCE: Chinese companies across mainland A-shares, Hong Kong listings and US-listed receipts, actively picked with technology the biggest slice. It spreads across China's listing venues in one fund, carrying the region's regulatory and currency risks.
SPUT: US stocks paired with a daily put-writing program that sells S&P 500 put options every day to collect premium income. The steady premium softens small drops and adds income, but a fast sell-off still hurts, and gains lag in strong rallies.
GGTL: Technology companies from around the world, chipmakers, software firms and electronics giants, picked actively by Gabelli. At nearly nine tenths technology it is a pure sector bet, so it rises and falls with the tech cycle.
PRTO: A tactical portfolio steered by trend and momentum signals, currently heavy in small-cap stock funds and gold, with some big-index exposure. The mix shifts as trends change, aiming to ride what is working and step aside from what is not.
EZPZ: Only two cryptocurrencies, bitcoin and ether, held in roughly their market proportions. It is the simplest crypto basket: no other coins, no stock exposure, and full exposure to the boom and bust mood of digital assets.
IBHM: High yield and lower-rated investment grade corporate bonds that mature during 2033, when the fund is scheduled to wrap up. Blending junk with BBB bonds lifts the income, and the fixed end date makes planning easier than with an open-ended bond fund.
XTJL: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each July. It is a leveraged-style bet on a rising market, with no cushion when the index falls.
QLVE: Emerging market stocks screened for quality and lower volatility, led by Asian technology, with finance, communications and energy behind. It aims for a calmer version of emerging market growth, though calmer is relative in markets that can drop fast.
SROI: Growth companies worldwide that also meet sustainability criteria, spanning technology, industry, finance and health care. It pairs a growth hunt with environmental and social screens, so some popular stocks are left out on principle.
QIG: Investment grade corporate bonds from US banks, hospitals, insurers and other issuers, selected for healthy fundamentals and income. It aims to be a core corporate bond holding with a quality tilt, avoiding the weakest borrowers in the market.
HCOW: Shares of a cash-flow-focused dividend fund, plus call options sold against that position to add a second layer of income. The double income design means high payouts, while the covered calls cap much of the growth when stocks rally.
JULH: Treasury bills paired with options on the S&P 500 that pay income as long as the index stays above a barrier set 20 percent below its starting level. If the index falls through the barrier, the fund takes on the market's losses instead.
CQTM: Companies building quantum computers and the security tools meant to withstand them, a small and speculative corner of technology. Holdings are concentrated in a few young companies, so single-stock news can drive the whole result.
TSLP: An options income strategy on a single stock, Tesla, using contracts on its shares while much of the fund sits in Treasury bills. It pays distributions from Tesla's famous volatility, with gains capped and full exposure to the stock's famous drops.
CLCV: Large US companies trading at value prices, drawn from the Russell 1000 Value universe across technology, finance, health care and industry. It owns some big tech names when they trade cheaply, so it is a value fund comfortable crossing style lines.
RNEM: Large and mid-sized emerging market companies selected from a broad index, with financial firms the biggest slice at over a third. It holds consumer, materials and technology names across Asia and beyond, carrying the usual currency and political risks of developing markets.
DQJN: Options on the Nasdaq-100 designed to gain from modest moves in either direction over a one-year period ending each June. It is built for a choppy tech market, while a strong one-way run, up or down, can leave it behind.
ESLV: Large US companies trading at value prices, balanced across finance, technology, industry and energy rather than concentrated in one sector. It is a steady, diversified value portfolio, the kind that tends to lag in go-go growth markets and hold up better in downturns.
TLTX: US Treasury bonds, held directly and through a Treasury ladder fund, with call options sold on Treasury funds to add income on top of interest. The options boost payouts in calm markets, while rate rises still push bond prices down.
EMFI: Dollar-denominated bonds from emerging market governments and companies, including higher-yielding frontier countries in Africa, Latin America and beyond. It pays more than developed-market debt, and its borrowers include governments with real default risk, so credit news matters a lot.
MEDX: Drugmakers and medical technology companies, from the biggest pharmaceutical firms to smaller research-driven names, mostly US and European. It is a concentrated health care portfolio, so drug trial results and pricing politics can move it more than the overall market.
LCDS: Large, established US companies chosen with a data-science-driven version of fundamental research, blending statistics with analyst judgment. Technology leads at about two fifths, making it a core holding with a growth tilt and an analytical edge as its claim to difference.
FEAC: US companies of every size, large, mid and small, picked with Fidelity's research into long-term return drivers like value, growth and quality. Technology is the biggest slice, and the all-cap reach means it holds some smaller names most large-cap funds skip.
TDEC: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each December. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
USAF: A multi-asset mix of property trusts, investment grade bonds, gold trusts and stocks from the US and abroad. It spreads money across assets that behave differently, aiming for balance rather than maximum growth, and gold gives it an inflation-sensitive streak.
GENZ: Digital-native companies: video game makers, e-commerce platforms, ride-hailing, online brokers and social apps from around the world. It is a growth bet on businesses born on the internet, spread across gaming, shopping, finance and media rather than one app category.
VDI: Dividend-paying companies outside the US, spread across at least eight countries, with financial firms the biggest slice at over two fifths. It hunts income abroad, so currency swings add to the ups and downs foreign stocks already bring.
LBAY: A long and short portfolio of income-producing alternatives to bonds, such as dividend stocks, preferred shares and property-related securities. Going both long and short aims to keep income flowing with smaller market swings, though it can lag when stocks climb steadily.
IVEP: Thirty companies supplying the power and infrastructure behind artificial intelligence: electrical equipment, data centers, cooling, utilities and energy firms. It is a picks-and-shovels bet on the AI buildout, profiting from spending on capacity rather than on any single AI winner.
RW: A focused portfolio of durable global companies, mostly mid and large sized, with industry and technology leading, picked for steady compounding. It holds a modest cash cushion and buys businesses meant to grow through good times and bad.
TACU: Core US stocks picked actively, spanning technology, finance, health care and communications in proportions close to the broad market. It aims to beat a plain index fund through research, while staying diversified enough to serve as a main holding.
TMAR: Options on a big emerging markets stock fund, structured with a buffer against the first slice of losses over a one-year period ending each March. It offers emerging market growth with a softer landing, while giving up part of the upside.
PCLN: Companies whose products clean up the planet: chip-making equipment, industrial technology, water and efficiency specialists from around the world. Technology and industry dominate, making it an environmental theme expressed through engineers rather than solar panels and wind farms.
LSEQ: Long and short positions in US stocks, buying companies the managers favor and betting against those they do not, across health care, materials and technology. The short side is meant to soften market drops, though it also trims gains in rallies.
UNL: Natural gas futures spread evenly across the next twelve months of contracts, rather than betting on the nearest month alone. Spreading the contracts softens the cost of rolling futures, and the fund still rides gas prices, which swing hard with the weather.
